title: How Leaders Overestimate and Underestimate Their Own Brain Power
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This entry applies the Dunning-Kruger effect to executive decision-making, describing how leaders routinely misjudge their own competence in both directions. In areas of genuine expertise, they can undervalue their own judgment and let less-informed voices carry too much weight. In unfamiliar territory, the opposite failure occurs: overconfidence crowds out input from people who actually know the subject. Because this bias is invisible to the person experiencing it, the piece argues the only reliable fix is external -- asking trusted colleagues where your expertise is real and where it is assumed. It closes with a Feynman quote as a reminder that self-deception is the easiest trap to fall into.
points: Leaders both overrate and underrate their own competence, depending on the domain.
In areas of real expertise, some leaders defer too much to less-qualified opinions.
In unfamiliar territory, overconfident leaders discount input from genuine experts.
Asking trusted colleagues to name your real strengths and gaps is the best corrective.
quotes: Leaders commonly overestimate their own thinking and brain power in areas where they lack expertise and underestimate their cognitive abilities on topics where they are highly competent.
Technically known as the Dunning-Kruger effect, this bias raises concerns about when leaders should trust their own instincts and abilities and when they shouldn’t.
In essence, some leaders weigh what others think way too much when they themselves are the true expert in the room.
Because it is invisible to those affected by it, this bias can severely skew an important decision.
Having a more objective view regarding your true expertise and skill is the most important step in combatting this pervasive bias.
The first principle is that you must not fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.
